readerTitle: Who is your candle really for?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (소규모 수제 양초 공방, 식단 계획 앱) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 작은 브랜드의 마케팅은 '누구에게 무엇을 약속할지' 먼저 정하고, 그다음 고객이 어디서 멈추는지 퍼널에서 찾는 두 단계로 풀린다.
misconception: 양초는 누구나 좋아하니 모두에게 알리고, 판매가 적으면 광고를 더 하면 된다.

factChecks.note: 양초 퍼널 계산: 방문 2,000 → 상품 조회 1,200 (60%) → 장바구니 300 (1,200의 25%) → 구매 30 (300의 10%). 가장 큰 이탈은 장바구니→구매 단계입니다.
배송비 비중: $9 ÷ $28 = 약 32%, 카드에는 'nearly a third'로 적었습니다.
앱 퍼널 계산: 다운로드 10,000 → 가입 4,000 (40%) → 첫 식단 3,000 (4,000의 75%) → 유료 150 (3,000의 5%). 비율이 가장 낮은 단계는 첫 식단→유료(5%)입니다.

cards.title: Who is your candle really for?
body: Mara pours 400 soy candles a month in a small rented workshop. She sells them for $28 at a weekend market, and people often say, "Everyone loves candles."
She wants to sell online and grow. That compliment is the first trap. A product for everyone gives her no clue who to talk to, or what to say.

image.label: A small workshop with candles cooling on a shelf
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 공방 작업대 위에 유리 용기 양초들이 식고 있고, 뒤쪽 선반에 포장 상자가 쌓여 있음. 따뜻한 조명. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Who should Mara market to first?
body: Mara looks at her market notes. Most repeat buyers are people buying a gift to bring when they're invited to dinner. Supermarkets sell factory candles for under $10.

options.text: Everyone who likes candles, with broad ads
options.feedback: Big reach, but a vague message. Without picking a **segment**, her $28 candle sits next to $10 ones with no reason to cost more.

options.text: Dinner guests buying a host gift, positioned as "the candle you bring to dinner"
options.feedback: This is **segment, target, position** at work. She picks the group she already serves best and gives them a clear reason to choose her.

options.text: Drop the price to $15 to win supermarket shoppers
options.feedback: It may win some buyers, but she fights factories on their strongest ground: cost. A small workshop rarely wins that race.

cards.title: One clear promise reshaped the product.
body: Once Mara chose host gifts, other decisions got easier. She added a gift-ready box and a small card for a note. She cut her scents from twelve to four that suit a dinner table.

Her online shop now says one thing: **the candle you bring to dinner**. People buying candles for themselves can still order. But every word, photo and box is built for the guest standing at a host's door.

image.label: A boxed candle with a gift card held at a front door
image.brief: 현관문 앞에서 손님이 리본 묶인 양초 선물 상자와 작은 메시지 카드를 들고 있는 장면. 따뜻한 저녁 분위기. 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: A month in her online shop.
body: Track each step a buyer takes, from first visit to payment. Each stage keeps a share of the one before it.

breakdown.label: Visit the shop
breakdown.detail: From social posts and market flyers

cards.title: Thirty sales. What does Mara fix first?
body: Glass jars are heavy and fragile, so shipping costs $9. Her shop shows that fee only on the last checkout screen. That's nearly a third of the candle's price.
Where should she spend her next week?

options.text: Buy more ads to double her visitors
options.feedback: More people would pour into the same leak. With only 10% of carts turning into sales, most of the extra spend would drain away.

options.text: Show shipping on the product page and offer free shipping on two candles
options.feedback: This is **the funnel** at work: fix the stage with the biggest drop first. It also nudges buyers toward two candles, which makes shipping cheaper per candle.

options.text: Add more scents to the product page
options.feedback: It might lift viewers into carts. But people already in the cart are leaving, and more choice doesn't fix a surprise fee.

cards.title: A clear position means saying no.
body: A gift shop asks to stock Mara's candles in a cheap bulk pack with no box. It's real money. It also blurs the promise she just built.

Positioning has a cost: you give up some sales to be the obvious choice for someone. And small numbers can mislead. Thirty sales can swing a lot from one month to the next, so watch the trend for a few months before you rebuild a step.

cards.title: Now it's a meal-planning app.
body: A small team runs a meal-planning app for "anyone who cooks." Each month: 10,000 downloads, 4,000 sign-ups, 3,000 make a first weekly plan, and 150 pay $6 a month. Most paying users are parents planning family dinners.
What should the team do next?

options.text: Run broad ads to double downloads
options.feedback: More downloads feed a funnel where only 5% of active planners pay. Volume hides the real problem instead of solving it.

options.text: Position the app for busy parents and fix the step from first plan to paying
options.feedback: Both ideas together: **segment, target, position** picks who to serve, and **the funnel** shows the weakest step is turning planners into payers.

options.text: Cut the price to $3 a month
options.feedback: It may lift the paying step a little, but it halves revenue per user and still speaks to no one in particular.

cards.softwareNote: In software, the funnel stages are often signup, first use and payment. The step where users first get value is usually the one worth fixing first.

cards.title: Choose who it's for, then find where they stop.
body: You used two ideas from this unit. **Segment, target, position** decided who Mara serves and what she promises. **The funnel** showed where buyers quit, so she fixed that step before buying more attention.
**Try it today:** name the one group your business serves best. Then count how many people reach each step before they pay, and circle the biggest drop.
